In Shakespeare's Macbeth, ambition begins as a dream and becomes a destructive force. At the start of the play, Macbeth is a loyal soldier, but after the witches tell him he will be king, he begins to think about how to get the crown. He says he has no reason to kill Duncan except 'vaulting ambition,' which shows he knows his desire is dangerous.

Lady Macbeth pushes his ambition even further. She calls him weak and tells him to be a man, and she plans the murder herself. After Duncan is killed, Macbeth becomes king, but he is not satisfied. He kills Banquo because he is afraid Banquo's children will be kings, and he sees Banquo's ghost at the feast.

By the end of the play, Macbeth has lost everything. Lady Macbeth goes mad and dies, and Macbeth says life is 'a tale told by an idiot.' He is killed by Macduff, and Malcolm becomes king. The play suggests that ambition without morals leads to ruin, and that getting power is not the same as being happy.
The theme of ambition is developed throughout Macbeth through the characters of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth. Their ambition drives the plot and leads to their downfall.

In Act 1, the witches greet Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor and future king. He is already Thane of Glamis, and soon he really does become Thane of Cawdor, which makes him believe the rest of the prophecy. Lady Macbeth reads his letter and says she fears his nature is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness' to take the shortcut to the crown. She calls on spirits to 'unsex' her so she can help. In Act 2, Macbeth sees a dagger in the air before he kills Duncan. In Act 3, he has Banquo murdered. In Act 5, Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and cannot wash the blood from her hands, saying 'Out, damned spot.'
All of these events show that ambition leads to crime and guilt. Macbeth and Lady Macbeth get what they want, but they lose their peace and their lives. Shakespeare shows that ambition is dangerous.

paragraphs: Shakespeare uses Macbeth to argue that ambition is not evil on its own, but becomes dangerous when it has no limits. Macbeth begins as a brave and respected man, and his first desire to be king is only a thought. What changes him is the decision to act on it without caring about right and wrong.

This idea is important because it means Macbeth is responsible for what happens. The witches only tell him what might happen; they never order him to kill anyone. He chooses to murder Duncan, and once he does that, he has to keep murdering to protect his position. Each crime leads to another, and his ambition grows into paranoia. By the end he trusts no one and is alone.

The play also shows that ambition can be shared and can spread. Lady Macbeth's desire for power is at least as strong as her husband's, and she helps him at the beginning. Later, though, her guilt overwhelms her while Macbeth becomes harder and colder. Their different paths show that ambition affects people in different ways.
In conclusion, the play suggests that ambition needs a moral limit. Without one, it destroys the person who has it and everyone around them.

paragraphs: Ambition is the main theme in Macbeth. It is developed in three parts, which are the rise, the crime, and the fall.

In the rise, Macbeth hears the witches predict he will be king. This plants the idea in his head. He is at first unsure, and says that if chance will have him king, chance may crown him without his stir. But then Duncan names his son Malcolm as heir, and Macbeth sees Malcolm as a obstacle. This is when his ambition starts to become dangerous.

In the crime, Macbeth kills Duncan with Lady Macbeth's help, and then kills Banquo and later Macduff's family. Each murder is worse then the one before. He is not fighting for a better kingdom, only to keep what he has taken.

In the fall, everyone turns against him. The English army come to Scotland, and Macduff, who was not born in the usual way, kills him. So Shakespeare seems to say that ambition eventually destroys people.
Overall, ambition in Macbeth starts small and ends very badly.

In Macbeth, Shakespeare shows how ambition can turn a good man into a tyrant. At first, Macbeth is described as 'brave Macbeth' and 'valor's minion' after the battle. He is honored by the king. But the witches' prophecy stirs a desire in him that he cannot stop thinking about.

Macbeth himself understands the danger. Before the murder he says he has 'no spur to prick the sides of my intent, but only vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself.' This means his ambition is like a rider who jumps too high and falls off the other side. Shakespeare is telling us that ambition can make people go too far.

After the murder of Duncan, he cannot enjoy being king. He says he is 'in blood stepped in so far' that going back would be as hard as going forward. So he keeps killing. Meanwhile Lady Macbeth's guilt makes her sleepwalk.

The play ends with Macbeth's death, and the country is free again. So the theme of ambition is that it starts as something good, becomes something bad, and finally ruins everything, including the person who had it.

Shakespeare develops the theme of ambition in Macbeth as a process of corruption, in which a desire that begins in the imagination gradually reshapes the person who holds it. The play suggests that ambition is not simply a wish for power but a force that consumes the moral sense of anyone who lets it take control.

The process begins in Act 1, when Macbeth is tempted by the witches' greeting. His reaction is telling: he is startled by a 'horrid image' that makes his heart pound, which shows that the idea of murder is already in his mind. Even then, he tries to resist. In Act 1, Scene 7 he lists reasons not to kill Duncan, admitting that Duncan is a good king and a guest in his house, and concludes that he has 'no spur' except 'vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself.' The image is of a rider who jumps too high and falls, and Macbeth knows it. Yet he goes on, which reveals that ambition has become stronger than his judgment.

After the murder, ambition changes from a desire into a need. Macbeth kills Banquo not because Banquo threatens him now, but because the prophecy said his sons would be kings, and his crown feels empty without a line of succession. He admits that he is 'in blood stepped in so far' that turning back would be as difficult as going on.

By the final act, ambition has emptied him. His 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow' speech describes life as meaningless. Shakespeare suggests that ambition without conscience can win a crown but destroys the ability to enjoy it.

In Macbeth, ambition is not presented as a single flaw but as a chain reaction. Shakespeare shows how one act done for power creates the need for the next, until the person who wanted to rise is trapped by what he has done.

The chain starts with a small step. After the witches' prophecy, Macbeth is unsure. He tells himself that if fate wants him to be king, it can crown him without any help from him. But once Duncan names Malcolm as his heir, Macbeth says the stars should hide their fires so that light will not see his 'black and deep desires.' The language of darkness shows that he already understands his ambition as something to hide.

The murder of Duncan ought to satisfy him, but it does not. Instead, he says 'to be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus,' which reveals the problem: power that is stolen is never secure. He orders the murder of Banquo, then later of Macduff's wife and children, actions that bring no benefit at all. The ambition that began as a desire to be king has turned into a fear of losing the crown.

Lady Macbeth follows a different path. She begins by asking to be filled 'top-full of direst cruelty,' but ends sleepwalking and trying to wash away imaginary blood. Her fall suggests that ambition cannot silence conscience forever.
Together, these arcs show that Shakespeare views ambition as self-defeating: the more Macbeth takes, the less he has.

paragraphs: Ambition in Macbeth develops from a private fantasy into a public tyranny, and the play suggests that it is dangerous because it feeds on itself. When Macbeth first meets the witches, he is surprised and even scared by his own thoughts. He says that the thought of murder 'shakes so my single state of man that function is smothered in surmise.' In other words, just thinking about it makes him unable to act normally. He is not yet a villain, only tempted.

Lady Macbeth accelerates the process. She sees that her husband has the desire but not the nerve, and she tells him that if he loves her he will 'screw your courage to the sticking-place.' She uses his love and his manhood to push him. Their plan shows that ambition can be encouraged by other people, not only come from inside.

Once Macbeth is king, the tone changes. He kills Banquo, and hires murderers, so that he doesnt have to get his own hands dirty. Later, he goes to the witches again, this time seeking certainty. They tell him no man born of woman can harm him, which makes him overconfident. The ambition which made him take the throne now makes him believe he is invincible, and this is what leads to his downfall when Macduff, born by cesarean, kills him.
Shakespeare's message seems to be that ambition, when it is unchecked, removes fear and conscience, but not consequences.

One of the most interesting choices Shakespeare makes in Macbeth is to let ambition grow in a world full of supernatural signs, so that we cannot easily say whether Macbeth is a victim of fate or of his own desire. Looking closely at how the theme develops, the play seems to argue for the second explanation.

The witches predict that Macbeth will be king, but they never tell him to kill. His reaction shows what is actually going on: he imagines the murder before anyone suggests it. The 'horrid image' that unfixes his hair is his own creation. Later, when he says 'stars, hide your fires,' he is asking nature itself to hide his intention, which shows that he knows it is wrong.

As the play continues, the connection between ambition and guilt becomes stronger. Macbeth cannot sleep, sees a dagger and then Banquo's ghost, and describes his mind as 'full of scorpions.' Each vision is a symptom of what the crime is doing to him. Shakespeare uses these images to show that ambition makes a person restless rather than satisfied.

By the end, the prophecies that once made Macbeth feel powerful trap him, since he misunderstands them. Birnam Wood does move, and Macduff was not born in the usual way. Shakespeare therefore suggests that ambition blinds people, so they hear only the promise and miss the warning.

Although Macbeth is a play about a man who wants a crown, the theme of ambition is developed most powerfully by comparing him with his wife. Shakespeare uses the two characters to show that ambition can look strong at first and hollow in the end.

At the beginning of the play, Lady Macbeth is the more ambitious of the two. When she reads Macbeth's letter, she worries that he is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness' and decides to help him overcome his conscience. Her speech asking spirits to 'unsex' her and fill her with cruelty shows that she thinks of ambition as something that requires giving up softer human qualities. Macbeth, in contrast, hesitates. He argues that killing Duncan is wrong, because Duncan is his king, his kinsman, and his guest.

Over the course of the play, their positions reverse. After the murder, Macbeth grows bolder, and tells his wife to be 'innocent of the knowledge' of the next crime. Lady Macbeth, in contrast, grows weaker. By Act 5 she is sleepwalking, rubbing her hands, and saying that all the perfumes of Arabia cannot sweeten them. Ambition has cost her the sleep and peace she once thought she could ignore.

This reversal suggests that Shakespeare sees ambition as a bargain that always takes more than it gives. Macbeth wins the throne, but by the end he calls life 'a tale told by an idiot,' full of sound and fury and meaning nothing.

Shakespeare's Macbeth does not simply warn that ambition is dangerous; it dramatizes how ambition changes a person's relation to time, language, and himself. Read closely, the play traces a movement from ambition as anticipation to ambition as exhaustion, and in doing so it questions whether the thing Macbeth wants can ever be had.

In the early acts, ambition lives in the future tense. Macbeth's first response to the witches is to be 'rapt' in thoughts of what 'shall be,' and his soliloquy in 1.7 hinges on the hope that the murder could 'trammel up the consequence.' He wants the deed done without its aftermath, an act that exists in a single moment. The speech ends with the image of 'vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself and falls on the other,' a rider who is so eager for the far side that he fails to land. Already the play suggests that ambition is a hunger for a result that ignores the road toward it.

Once the crown is his, that future-tense desire collapses into anxiety. 'To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus,' he says, and the line reveals what has happened: attaining the throne has not satisfied him, only created new things to lose. His obsession with Banquo's heirs, who will inherit what he cannot pass on, turns ambition from a wish for the present into a fear of the future.

The famous speech in Act 5 completes the pattern. Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in 'this petty pace,' and life becomes a 'walking shadow.' Ambition, which was always about the next day, has left him with nothing but days. Shakespeare's implication is bleak and precise: the ambitious person spends the present in pursuit of a future, and so ends without either.

A common reading of Macbeth holds that the play condemns ambition itself. A closer look suggests something more interesting: Shakespeare distinguishes between ambition that serves a person and ambition that serves a community, and it is this distinction, not ambition alone, that determines who is destroyed.

Macbeth's ambition is private from the start. Even in his moment of doubt, his reasons for not killing Duncan are all about consequences to himself, such as judgment 'here upon this bank and shoal of time,' and his only motive for going ahead is 'vaulting ambition.' Nothing in his desire concerns Scotland. Not surprisingly, the kingdom deteriorates as he holds it. Ross observes that the country 'cannot be called our mother, but our grave,' and the imagery of disorder, from unnatural storms to horses eating each other, ties his crime to the state of the land.

Against him, the play sets characters who seek power in a different way. Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty by pretending to be even worse than Macbeth, and only accepts the crown when he is sure that his aim is to heal Scotland, not to possess it. Macduff leaves his family to serve the country and mourns them as a man rather than as a soldier. Their ambition, if it can be called that, is answerable to something outside themselves.

Seen this way, the play's conclusion is not that people should never want power. Rather, Shakespeare shows that ambition without any obligation to others becomes self-consuming. Macbeth ends alone, surrounded by a country that wants him dead, and his final defiant fight is less a victory than a confirmation of what he has become.

In Macbeth, ambition is developed less through argument than through image. Shakespeare gives the theme a pattern of vocabulary, of darkness, blood, clothing, and sleep, that lets the audience watch ambition change what it touches. By following these images from the beginning of the play to the end, we can see that ambition is presented as a process of self-estrangement.

Clothing is one of the most telling motifs. When Macbeth is named Thane of Cawdor, he protests that the honor is 'borrowed robes,' and later he feels his kingship 'hang loose about him, like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief.' The image is precise: what ambition acquires does not fit the person who acquired it. He wants the identity of a king but has earned only the costume.

Darkness works in a similar way. Macbeth asks the stars to hide their fires and Lady Macbeth calls on night to cover her actions in smoke, because both know that the desire cannot bear inspection. Yet the more they conceal, the less they can rest. Sleep, which Macbeth believes he has murdered, becomes the price of the crime. By Act 5, Lady Macbeth's compulsion to keep a light beside her shows that the darkness they invited has turned against them.

Finally, the blood imagery reverses. Macbeth first thinks that water can wash his hands clean; he later sees that his hand would instead make the seas 'incarnadine.' Lady Macbeth's 'Out, damned spot' shows the same lesson: the deed cannot be undone. The play is therefore pessimistic about ambition, since it shows that its rewards are borrowed, its methods are concealed, and its consequences are permanent.

Any account of ambition in Macbeth has to reckon with the witches, since it is tempting to blame them. If supernatural beings promise a man a crown, is his ambition his own? Shakespeare's answer, developed carefully across the first three acts, is that the prophecy reveals ambition more than it creates it.

Notice first what the witches actually say. They hail Macbeth by titles, and they predict, but they never suggest a method. Banquo hears the same prophecy and responds with suspicion, warning that evil often tells small truths to betray us in deeper matters. Macbeth's reaction is different in kind: he is 'rapt,' and he imagines murder at once. The contrast with Banquo is the key. Two men are offered the same temptation, and only one is drawn to act, which shows that the difference lies within the person and not the prophecy.

The play also refuses to let Macbeth hide behind fate. In the soliloquy in Act 1, Scene 7, he lists the reasons against the murder, and he concedes that the only thing pushing him forward is 'vaulting ambition.' By this point he is not deceived; he understands the wrong and chooses it. Later, when he returns to the witches for guidance, he has already decided that he will act, and he wants prophecies that will excuse him.

The tragedy, then, is not that Macbeth was manipulated but that he was free. Shakespeare shows ambition as a choice that becomes a habit: the more Macbeth acts, the fewer choices appear to remain, until he says returning would be 'as tedious as go o'er.' The theme is thus less about destiny than about the way a chosen desire turns into a condition.

Shakespeare's Macbeth is often read as a story about a single man's overreaching, but the play develops ambition as something contagious and reciprocal, passing between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth, and finally exhausting both. This shared structure makes the play's judgment on ambition more troubling: it is not a private vice but a relationship that can corrupt what it should protect.

At the outset, ambition is a shared language of encouragement. Lady Macbeth greets her husband's letter by resolving to 'chastise with the valour of my tongue' whatever stands between him and the crown, and she makes his hesitation a question of identity, asking whether he is 'afraid to be the same in thine own act and valour as thou art in desire.' The two are bound by love as much as greed, and their marriage becomes the vehicle for their plan.

Yet the same bond is the first casualty of success. After Duncan's murder, Macbeth begins to keep secrets from her, telling her to be 'innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck,' before Banquo's murder. The partners who once spoke as one now speak past each other. When Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, she is alone with her guilt, and Macbeth receives the news of her death with the flat remark that she 'should have died hereafter.' What ambition promised as a joint triumph divides them.

The final movement of the play shows the cost. Macbeth has the crown, but not the companion, not the sleep, and not the future. Shakespeare's suggestion is that ambition is dangerous precisely because it seems to be a way of gaining everything, while it quietly spends the things that give gaining any meaning.
